'''Hsu Yun-chi''' (Chinese: 許雲基; 16 July 1924 – 2025) was a Taiwanese [[nuclear physicist]] from [[Taichung]], Taiwan.<ref name="Dialogue Spring Travel"/><ref name="Early NTU Nuclear Physics Laboratory Again">{{cite journal |author=Zheng Bokun |title=The Early NTU Nuclear Physics Laboratory Revisited |url=http://psroc.phys.ntu.edu.tw/bimonth/download.php?d=1&cpid=33&did=3 |journal=Physics Bimonthly |publisher=[[Physical Society of the Republic of China]] |date=February 1999 |volume=29 |issue=1 |language=zh-tw |pages=23–35 |access-date=14 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150814130937/http://psroc.phys.ntu.edu.tw/bimonth/download.php?d=1&cpid=33&did=3 |archive-date=14 August 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{rp|34}} After graduating from [[Taichung First Senior High School]], Hsu studied at [[Kochi High School]] in Japan and then at the Faculty of Engineering of [[Kyoto Imperial University]]. After the war, he transferred to the Department of Electrical Engineering at [[National Taiwan University]] and graduated from that department.<ref name="Ministry of Culture"/><ref name="Zhang Xingzhen">{{cite thesis |author=Zhang Xingzhen |date=31 July 2003 |title=The Transformation of Knowledge Communities in Taiwan: From the Physics Chairs of Taihoku Imperial University to the Department of Physics of National Taiwan University |pages=20 |url=http://ndltd.ncl.edu.tw/cgi-bin/gs32/gsweb.cgi?o=dnclcdr&s=id=%22091NTU00493013%22.&searchmode=basic |access-date=11 June 2012 |language=zh-tw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150628071851/http://ndltd.ncl.edu.tw/cgi-bin/gs32/gsweb.cgi?o=dnclcdr&s=id%3D%22091NTU00493013%22.&searchmode=basic |archive-date=28 June 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{rp|161}}

In 1947, Hsu became an assistant in the [[Department of Physics, National Taiwan University]]. Together with [[Dai Yungui]], [[Ota Yoritsune]] and others, he helped reconstruct the [[Cockcroft–Walton generator]] built at NTU by the team of [[Bunsaku Arakatsu]], which had previously completed the world's second artificial nuclear disintegration experiment. In 1948, the group successfully completed the first artificial nuclear disintegration experiment in [[Taiwan]] and in post-war Asia. He later took over the nuclear physics laboratory led by Ota Yoritsune,<ref name="Lin Xiayu"/> and led Taiwanese technicians in repeatedly improving the laboratory's equipment,<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|166}} making it one of Asia's most advanced nuclear laboratories in the 1960s.<ref name="Digital Archive of the History of Physics in Taiwan"/>{{rp|4}}<ref name="New Living Water"/>{{rp|99–100}} Hsu was promoted from assistant to lecturer, associate professor and professor, and became chair of the NTU Department of Physics in 1962.<ref name="Department Chairs"/> He retired from the NTU Department of Physics in 1985 and became professor emeritus in 1989.<ref name="Digital Archive of the History of Physics in Taiwan"/>{{rp|15,21}}<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|180}} Beginning in 2005, he led the reconstruction of the nuclear physics laboratory into the [[NTU Museum of Physics]].<ref name="Nuclear Physics"/><ref name="Nuclear Physics Laboratory"/><ref name="Hi NTU"/>{{rp|151}}

== Life ==

=== Early life ===
Hsu Yun-chi was born in 1924 in Waipu Village, Dajia District, Taichū Prefecture, [[Taiwan under Japanese rule]].{{efn|Now [[Waipu District]], [[Taichung]].}}<ref name="Dialogue Spring Travel"/> After graduating from Taichung Prefectural First Middle School<ref name="Ministry of Culture">{{cite web |access-date=8 December 2025 |title=Hsu Yun-chi — National Cultural Memory Bank |publisher=[[National Museum of Taiwan History]] |url=https://tcmb.culture.tw/zh-tw/detail?indexCode=Culture_People&id=553144 }}; {{cite web |access-date=8 December 2025 |title=Hsu Yun-chi |publisher=Ministry of Culture, Republic of China |author=Li Kaiyang |url=https://cmsdb.culture.tw/person/EBACFF9C-37B5-4C86-BF4F-7EA2EA45EA92 }}</ref>—today [[Taichung First Senior High School]]<ref name="Lin Xiayu"/>—he went to Japan to study at [[Kochi High School]].<ref name="Ministry of Culture"/><ref name="Ministry of Culture High School">{{cite web |access-date=8 December 2025 |title=Photograph of NTU Physics Professor Hsu Yun-chi During His High School Studies — National Cultural Memory Bank |publisher=[[National Museum of Taiwan History]] |url=https://tcmb.culture.tw/zh-tw/detail?indexCode=Culture_Object&id=599306 }}; {{cite web |access-date=8 December 2025 |title=Photograph of NTU Physics Professor Hsu Yun-chi During His High School Studies |publisher=Ministry of Culture, Republic of China |author=Li Kaiyang |url=https://cmsdb.culture.tw/object/BF5BD8D7-5324-43C7-A007-284779D5C3B1 }}</ref> After graduating, he was admitted to the Faculty of Engineering of [[Kyoto Imperial University]].<ref name="Ministry of Culture"/> While studying there, he attended courses taught by [[Bunsaku Arakatsu]] and learned that [[Kiichi Kimura]] and others in the university's [[atomic nucleus]] laboratory were conducting nuclear experiments.<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|161}}

After [[World War II]], Hsu transferred from the Department of Electrical Engineering at Kyoto Imperial University to the Department of Electrical Engineering at NTU,<ref name="Ministry of Culture"/><ref name="Lin Xiayu"/> graduating in the summer of 1947.<ref name="Dialogue Spring Travel"/><ref name="Ministry of Culture"/> Shortly before graduation, Zhang Tiaoxu, an assistant in the Department of Chemistry and Hsu's classmate at Taichung First Senior High School, recommended him to the nuclear disintegration experimental group of the [[Department of Physics, National Taiwan University]].<ref name="Ministry of Culture"/> Associate professor [[Ota Yoritsune]] hoped that Hsu would report for duty the day after graduation.<ref name="Science Monthly"/>{{rp|914}} Hsu, however, first returned to his family home in Dajia for a period of rest and did not return to [[Taipei]] until late September, formally beginning work in the NTU Department of Physics in October.<ref name="Dialogue Spring Travel"/><ref name="Lin Xiayu"/><ref name="Chinese Journal for the History of Science and Technology"/>{{rp|157}} For this, Hsu received a severe reprimand.<ref name="Science Monthly"/>{{rp|914}} According to Xu Zhongping, Hsu Yun-chi was gentle and modest, and often unconsciously covered his mouth with one hand while speaking, a habit he retained into old age.<ref name="Science Monthly"/>{{rp|914}}

=== Career at the NTU Department of Physics ===
[[File:臺大物理文物廳展覽廳.jpg|200px|right|thumb|The Cockcroft–Walton linear particle accelerator now displayed at the [[NTU Museum of Physics]].]]
[[File:NTUNuclearExp1948.png|200px|thumb|Members of the NTU Department of Physics nuclear laboratory: Xu Dongtang, Zhou Muchun, Hsu Yun-chi, Liu Yuanzhong, Lin Songyun and Xu Yuchuan.]]

After Hsu reported to Ota Yoritsune in October 1947 and became an assistant in the department, Ota arranged for him to live in a red-brick house behind the meteorological building. Hsu first repaired the department's [[Geiger counter]] and then began learning vacuum techniques.<ref name="Lin Xiayu">{{Cite journal |author=Lin Xiayu |title=Carbon-14 Isotope Dating |journal=NTU Alumni Bimonthly |issue=45 |publisher=National Taiwan University |url=http://www.alum.ntu.edu.tw/wordpress/?p=1043 |date=1 May 2006 |access-date=18 July 2015 |language=zh-tw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150718040139/http://www.alum.ntu.edu.tw/wordpress/?p=1043 |archive-date=18 July 2015 |url-status=dead }}; {{cite web |access-date=8 December 2025 |title=NTU Alumni Bimonthly |url=http://ntualumnibm.ntu.edu.tw/bm.bimonthly.article/detail/sn/2592 |publisher=NTU Alumni Association }}</ref><ref name="Chinese Journal for the History of Science and Technology">{{Cite journal |author=[[Liu Guangding]] |year=2010 |title=The First Nuclear Reaction Completed in China |journal=Chinese Journal for the History of Science and Technology |volume=31 |issue=2 |issn=1673-1441 |publisher=China Association for Science and Technology |location=[[Beijing]] |pages=153–164 |url=http://www.cqvip.com/QK/91361A/201002/34210080.html |access-date=18 July 2015 |language=zh-cn |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/6a6aUfyAw?url=http://www.cqvip.com/QK/91361A/201002/34210080.html |archive-date=18 July 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{rp|157}}<ref name="Newsletter for the History of Science"/>{{rp|53}}<ref name="Chinese Science and Technology"/>{{rp|8,10}}

Hsu then followed Dai Yungui and Ota Yoritsune, working with [[Kawada Suekichi]] and Taiwanese technicians including [[Xu Yuchuan]], Zhou Mucun and Lin Songyun, to reassemble the [[Cockcroft–Walton generator]] made at NTU by Arakatsu's team, which had completed the world's second artificial nuclear disintegration experiment.{{efn|For details of this event, see [[Bunsaku Arakatsu]].}}<ref name="Digital Archive of the History of Physics in Taiwan">{{cite web |url=http://ntur.lib.ntu.edu.tw/bitstream/246246/77859/1/952422H002015.pdf |language=zh-tw |title=Digital Archive Project for the History of Physics in Taiwan |publisher=[[National Science Council]] of the [[Executive Yuan]] |date=29 March 2007 |access-date=27 January 2015 |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/6ZcOMqGof?url=http://ntur.lib.ntu.edu.tw/bitstream/246246/77859/1/952422H002015.pdf |archive-date=28 June 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{rp|21}}<ref name="Hi NTU">{{cite book |author=Liu Ziming |author2=Yang Songhan|author3= Cai Mingda|author4=Liu Jianfu |title=Hi! NTU: Decoding 82 Keys to National Taiwan University |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Lxl578rOVhYC&pg=PA149 |publisher=[[National Taiwan University Press]] |location=[[Taipei]] |isbn=978-986-02-2869-4 |date=April 2010 |access-date=3 December 2014 |language=zh-tw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150128172924/http://books.google.com.tw/books?id=Lxl578rOVhYC&pg=PA149&hl=zh-TW&source=gbs_toc_r&cad=3#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=28 January 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Newsletter for the History of Science">{{cite journal |author=Liu Guangding |date=March 2009 |title=Historical Facts Revisited: The First Nuclear Fission Experiment Completed by National Taiwan University Sixty Years Ago |url=http://www4.isu.edu.tw/sites/chsas_taipei/doc/add_32.pdf |access-date=2 November 2014 |journal=Newsletter for the History of Science |volume=32 |language=zh-tw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150122090542/http://www4.isu.edu.tw/sites/chsas_taipei/doc/add_32.pdf |archive-date=22 January 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{rp|53}}

To obtain sufficient experimental materials, they borrowed from the better-supplied Department of Chemistry and obtained discarded [[vacuum tube]]s, large shell casings and other items from the [[Broadcasting Corporation of China]] and [[Taiwan Power Company]].<ref name="Science Monthly">{{Cite journal |author=Xu Zhongping |date=December 1993 |title=Hsu Yun-chi and Taiwan's First Nuclear Disintegration Experiment |journal=[[Science Monthly]] |volume=24 |issue=12 |publisher=Science Monthly Magazine |pages=913–917 |language=zh-tw }}{{cite web |access-date=8 December 2025 |title=1993 Vol. 24 No. 12, Issue 288 — Science Monthly Fifty-Year Collection |url=https://smcase.ntu.edu.tw/SMCASE/?p=3317 |publisher=NTU Science Education Center |archive-date=8 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250908034937/https://smcase.ntu.edu.tw/SMCASE/?p=3317 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{rp|914}}

The accelerator reconstruction project began in October 1946.<ref name="Chinese Science and Technology">{{Cite journal |author=Liu Guangding |date=December 2006 |title=A Preliminary Study of Nuclear Science in China, 1945–1948 |journal=Journal of the Chinese Society for the History of Science and Technology |issue=10 |pages=7–10 |url=http://readopac2.ncl.edu.tw/nclJournal/search/detail.jsp?dtdId=000040&search_type=detail&la=ch&checked=&unchecked=&sysId=0006558169 |access-date=26 January 2015 |language=zh-tw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402104521/http://readopac2.ncl.edu.tw/nclJournal/search/detail.jsp?dtdId=000040&search_type=detail&la=ch&checked=&unchecked=&sysId=0006558169 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |url-status=live }}; {{Cite journal |author=Liu Guangding |author-link=Liu Guangding |title=A Preliminary Study of Nuclear Science in China, 1945–1948 |url=http://www.sciencehistory.url.tw/wp-content/uploads/2008/09/10_2.pdf |url-status=live |language=zh |journal=Journal of the Chinese Society for the History of Science and Technology |date=December 2006 |issue=10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240619181622/http://www.sciencehistory.url.tw/wp-content/uploads/2008/09/10_2.pdf |archive-date=19 June 2024 }}{{rp|6–17}}; {{cite journal |access-date=6 December 2025 |date=December 2006 |title=A Preliminary Study on the Nuclear Science in China, 1945–48 |publisher=Airiti Library |url=https://www.airitilibrary.com/Article/Detail/a0000577-200612-201005190054-201005190054-6-14 |author=Liu Guangding |journal=中華科技史學會會刊 |issue=10 |pages=6–14 |doi=10.7094/BAHS.200612.0006 }}{{rp|6–14}}</ref>{{rp|8}} On 13 May 1948 at 8:35 p.m., the team used high-speed [[proton]]s to strike [[lithium]], splitting it into two [[alpha particle]]s and completing the first artificial nuclear disintegration experiment in Taiwan and post-war Asia.<ref name="Digital Archive of the History of Physics in Taiwan"/>{{rp|4}}<ref name="Early NTU Nuclear Physics Laboratory Again"/>{{rp|24}}<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|161–162}}<ref name="New Living Water"/>{{rp|99}}<ref name="Nuclear Physics Laboratory">{{cite web |url=http://web.phys.ntu.edu.tw/gphyslab/physmu/nuclear.html |title=Nuclear Physics Laboratory |publisher=[[NTU Museum of Physics]] |access-date=2 December 2014 |language=zh-tw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150604004614/http://web.phys.ntu.edu.tw/gphyslab/physmu/nuclear.html |archive-date=4 June 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Newsletter for the History of Science"/>{{rp|53}}<ref name="Chinese Science and Technology"/>{{rp|6}} On 20 June of the same year, they repeated the experiment and confirmed the reproducibility of the results.<ref name="Newsletter for the History of Science"/>{{rp|53}}<ref name="Chinese Science and Technology"/>{{rp|6}}

To keep pace with the work, Hsu left his newly married wife at his family home in Dajia and often slept overnight in the laboratory with Ota Yoritsune, Xu Yuchuan and Lin Songyun, continuing work after waking.<ref name="Dialogue Spring Travel">{{cite news |title=Dialogue Spring Travel: The 92-Year-Old Taiwanese Physicist Hsu Yuin-Chi — Green Hills Remain, While Several Sunsets Pass |url=http://news.cnair.com/c/201402/53347.html |language=zh-cn |author=Zhou Hua |publisher=China Aviation Tourism Network |date=13 February 2014 |access-date=19 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150719143328/http://news.cnair.com/c/201402/53347.html |archive-date=19 July 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="New Living Water">{{Cite journal |title=Days Walking with the Atomic Grandfathers: Notes on Filming the Restoration Documentary of the NTU Nuclear Laboratory |author=Zhang Xingzhen |url=http://www.gacc.org.tw/archive/magazine/5paw5rS75rC0IOWJteWIiuiZny5wZGYhfiEyMDEzLTA5LTI2IDIwOjIwOjEz.pdf |journal=New Living Water Bimonthly |date=July 2005 |publisher=[[General Association of Chinese Culture]] |language=zh-tw |pages=98–101 |issue=1 |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/6alvW5C29?url=http://www.gacc.org.tw/archive/magazine/5paw5rS75rC0IOWJteWIiuiZny5wZGYhfiEyMDEzLTA5LTI2IDIwOjIwOjEz.pdf |archive-date=14 August 2015 |url-status=dead |access-date=16 August 2015 }}</ref>{{rp|100}} The accelerator is now displayed by [[National Taiwan University]] in the [[NTU Museum of Physics]], the former nuclear laboratory of the physics chair.<ref name="Nuclear Physics Laboratory"/> Recalling the construction of the accelerator, Hsu said, “Hey! How did we have so much energy back then?”<ref name="New Living Water"/>{{rp|100}} When asked whether they feared electric leakage and radiation from the accelerator, he replied:

{{blockquote|We were terribly afraid, but it seems we did not die. When the first experiment succeeded in striking lithium atoms, we watched with our eyes. When the rays came out, we were so excited that we used no shielding at all. But everyone lived into their seventies or eighties, and it seems nothing happened.<ref name="New Living Water"/>{{rp|100}}}}

In 1949, after Ota Yoritsune was affected by the [[February 28 incident]] and repatriated to Japan by the [[Government of the Republic of China]],<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|164}} Hsu took over Ota's laboratory.<ref name="Lin Xiayu"/> He then led Taiwanese technicians in repeatedly improving the nuclear physics laboratory.<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|166}} First, his team built a [[Wilson cloud chamber]] to observe [[alpha particle]] tracks, improving on Ota's earlier apparatus, which could observe but not record the tracks.<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|167}} They then modified the accelerator to produce high-energy neutrons and raise the level of nuclear reactions. Using [[helium-4]] reactions, they produced 14.1 [[MeV]] high-energy [[neutron]]s to study induced nuclear reactions.<ref name="Lin Xiayu"/> Hsu's team also converted the accelerator's [[ion source]] into an [[RF antenna ion source]], and later thoroughly rebuilt the accelerator into a [[heavy ion]] accelerator for ion [[sputtering]] experiments.<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|167}} In addition, the research team used a mercury rectifier tube made from a [[Pyrex]] beaker and discarded high-power vacuum-tube electrodes from the Broadcasting Corporation of China to produce heavy water. After about a year of effort, they successfully produced 98% heavy water.<ref name="Lin Xiayu"/>

On 1 March 1954, the United States tested a [[hydrogen bomb]] at [[Bikini Atoll]], causing serious radioactive contamination in nearby waters. Contaminated fish from the area were transported back to Taiwan. The Taiwan Provincial Fishermen's Association, now the [[National Fishermen's Association, Republic of China]], brought the fish to the lobby of NTU Building No. 2, where they were tested for radioactivity using a Geiger counter made by Xu's team.<ref name="Early NTU Nuclear Physics Laboratory Again"/>

In the 1960s, Hsu's team began making [[carbon-14]] detectors,<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|169}} mainly to understand the influence of post-war atmospheric [[nuclear test]]ing on radioactivity in Taiwanese [[rice]]. They found that the radiocarbon content of Taiwanese trees was higher than that of European trees.<ref name="Lin Xiayu"/> At the time, the team used [[radiocarbon dating]] to assist the NTU Department of Archaeology and Anthropology, now the Department of Anthropology, with artifact identification and the Department of Geology with fossil and stratigraphic research.<ref name="Lin Xiayu"/><ref name="Nuclear Physics"/><ref name="Spacetime 1967">{{cite journal |title=Overview of Research and Development in the NTU Department of Physics |journal=Spacetime |issue=5 |year=1967 |language=zh-tw |publisher=NTU Department of Physics Student Association |access-date=20 August 2015 |pages=1–6 |url=http://web.phys.ntu.edu.tw/physhistory/spacetime/vol_05/v5_p1.pdf |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/6awbEcxun?url=http://web.phys.ntu.edu.tw/physhistory/spacetime/vol_05/v5_p1.pdf |archive-date=21 August 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{rp|3–4}} The team was the only group in Taiwan with this technology at the time.<ref name="Dialogue Spring Travel"/> The dating of the [[Changbin culture]] site was completed during this period by the team led by Hsu.<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|169}}<ref name="Nuclear Physics"/> They also hoped to use the technique to measure changes in [[cosmic ray]]s.<ref name="Spacetime 1967"/>{{rp|3–4}}

The research by Hsu's team made the NTU Department of Physics nuclear laboratory one of Asia's most advanced nuclear laboratories in the 1960s, and the team published nearly thirty papers.<ref name="Digital Archive of the History of Physics in Taiwan"/>{{rp|4}}<ref name="New Living Water"/>{{rp|99–100}} In 1961, Hsu, then an associate professor, received funding from the [[International Atomic Energy Agency]] to conduct a two-year research project at the Japan Atomic Energy Research Institute in [[Tokai, Ibaraki]].<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|168}}<ref name="Spacetime 1991">{{cite journal |title=A Brief History of Research and Development in the NTU Department of Physics |journal=Spacetime |issue=26 |date=September 1991 |author1=Chen Zhenghong |author2=Liu Zhenchen |language=zh-tw |publisher=NTU Department of Physics Student Association |access-date=20 August 2015 |pages=6–13 |url=http://web.phys.ntu.edu.tw/physhistory/spacetime/vol_26/index.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150821074324/http://web.phys.ntu.edu.tw/physhistory/spacetime/vol_26/index.htm |archive-date=21 August 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{rp|8}} During his career at the NTU Department of Physics, Hsu advanced through publications from assistant to lecturer, associate professor and professor, and became department chair in October 1962.<ref name="Department Chairs">{{cite web |title=Past Chairs of the NTU Department of Physics |url=http://www.phys.ntu.edu.tw/guide/powerman.aspx |publisher=[[Department of Physics, National Taiwan University]] |date=25 March 2015 |language=zh-tw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150802025014/http://www.phys.ntu.edu.tw/guide/powerman.aspx |archive-date=2 August 2015 |url-status=live |access-date=16 August 2015 }}</ref> In 1965, when Taiwan's National Science Council established a Physics Research Center, Hsu and [[Wolfgang Kroll]] became chair professors representing the NTU Department of Physics at the center.<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|167}}

=== Later years ===
[[File:NTU PhysicsOldBuilding.JPG|200px|thumb|The Taihoku Imperial University physics and chemistry classroom building, completed on 3 May 1931.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lib.ntu.edu.tw/gallery/pdf/03-05-03_校史紀事.pdf |language=zh-tw |title=Chronicle of National Taiwan University History |publisher=NTU History Gallery |date=13 November 2012 |access-date=26 February 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140903071101/http://www.lib.ntu.edu.tw/gallery/pdf/03-05-03_%E6%A0%A1%E5%8F%B2%E7%B4%80%E4%BA%8B.pdf |archive-date=3 September 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref> It houses the [[NTU Museum of Physics]], formerly the nuclear laboratory.]]

Hsu retired from the NTU Department of Physics in 1985 and, in 1989, became professor emeritus together with [[Wolfgang Kroll]].<ref name="Digital Archive of the History of Physics in Taiwan"/>{{rp|15,21}}<ref name="Zhang Xingzhen"/>{{rp|180}} After his retirement, the accelerator was dismantled because of a lack of space in the nuclear physics laboratory. Technicians Lin Songyun and Xu Yuchuan, unwilling to abandon it, hid its parts in various places for nearly twenty years.<ref name="Nuclear Physics Laboratory"/><ref name="Hi NTU"/>{{rp|151}} The two even stored the parts in warehouses, basements and bathroom ceilings.<ref name="New Living Water"/>{{rp|100–101}}<ref name="Nuclear Physics">{{cite web |title=NTU Museum of Physics: Nuclear Physics — People and History |url=http://web.phys.ntu.edu.tw/gphyslab/nuphys/DeHistoryPlace_1.html |language=zh-tw |publisher=[[NTU Museum of Physics]] |access-date=24 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150604034325/http://web.phys.ntu.edu.tw/gphyslab/nuphys/DeHistoryPlace_1.html |archive-date=4 June 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2004, the NTU Department of Physics decided to reconstruct the accelerator. Beginning in 2005, Hsu, together with Lin Songyun and Xu Yuchuan, led the reconstruction of the nuclear physics laboratory into the [[NTU Museum of Physics]], which officially opened on 21 November that year.<ref name="Nuclear Physics"/><ref name="Nuclear Physics Laboratory"/><ref name="Hi NTU"/>{{rp|151}} The reconstruction process was made into the documentary ''Breaking Through the Atomic Nucleus''.<ref name="Digital Archive of the History of Physics in Taiwan"/>{{rp|9,21}} Hsu summarized his thirty-eight-year teaching career by saying: “It was a very difficult era, but everyone was very serious.”<ref name="Lin Xiayu"/>
